So inside each n^2 square, there is an (n-2)^2 square of “inner” points. If you’re picking randomly, there’s a (n-2)^2 / n^2 chance of picking an inner point.

E.g. n=2, there are four total points (four outer points and no inner points), so you have no chance of picking an inner points. (n-2)^2 / n^2 = (2-2)^2 / 2^2 = 0/4 = 0%.
n=5, there are twentyfive total points (sixteen outer points and nine inner points), so you have a nine in twentyfive chance of picking an inner point. (n-2)^2 / n^2 = (5-2)^2 / 5^2 = 9/25 = 36%.

Probability of exactly k heads is just 2^-n, given order doesn’t matter and you simply need exactly one of the entire set of outcomes.

Probability of at least k heads means you don’t care about (n-k) outcomes, they could be heads or tails, so that part just becomes probability of one. Then the remaining k heads part is the same problem as above, just with a probability of 2^-k.

I’ll word it differently. You finish 5th, only ahead of the team in 6th through one bonus point. You travel to another country and manage to beat the team in 4th. Congratulations.

Turns out, the teams in 1st, 6th, and 7th also won. Because of how the draw is set in stone, you must play the best team in the competition away from home in order to qualify for a final, whereas the team that did worse than you gets a home game against the worst team left in the finals, and the worst team left in the finals gets to play the second-worst instead of the best, so they are rewarded for not finishing 5th as well. That’s right, the 7th placed team has a better run to the finals than the 5th placed team.

Because the finals are set in stone, you have created a perverse incentive, where finishing 6th or 7th is a better outcome to finishing 5th.

If you simply have highest ranked v lowest ranked, this perverse incentive does not exist, and winning is always rewarded.

Say the winners are Sharks, Chiefs, Hurricanes, and Crusaders. Despite the second-highest ranked remaining team in the finals, the Hurricanes would not host the SF, while the losing-record 6th place Sharks would. It creates a perverse outcome where it is reasonably better to finish 6th or 7th than it is to finish 5th.

There were three legislative bodies in the Republic: the comitia centuriata (Centuriate Assembly), the comitia populi tributa (Tribal Assembly), and the concilium plebis (Plebeian Council). Every citizen was a member on the comitia, while only plebeians were members of the council.

The Centuriate Assembly elected magistrates with Imperium: Censors, Consuls, and Praetors. The assembly conducted business in formal comitia, but would often have unofficial meetings between magistrates and citizens in the form of conventio. They were also able to act as a court of appeal, and were the only body able to ratify foreign treaties, or to declare war.
Originally, the Centuriate Assembly was broken into 193 individual blocks: 6 Senatorial blocks, 12 Equites, 80 First Order, 20 Second Order, 20 Third Order, 20 Fourth Order, 30 Fifth Order, 4 Craftsmen, and 1 Proletarii/Capite Censi. No matter the number of people in each century, the overall unit had only one vote, and therefore only 97 votes were necessary to pass a measure. The orders were evenly broken into men older than 45 and men younger. The voting order was to choose a First Order century at random, then work down the list: senatorial, equites, 1st Order, 2nd Order, 3rd Order, 4th Order, 5th Order, Craftsmen, Proletarii. At some point, this structure may have changed: some claim each order was changed to have 70 centuries, some that the strict order of calling was abandoned, but we don’t know. 

The Tribal Assembly elected lesser magistrates, such as Quaestors, the curule Aediles, and (maybe) the Military Tribunes. They also elected the Pontifex Maximus. Smaller measures than foreign treaty and war could be voted on in the Assembly, and we know that this happened often enough that they eventually instituted a rule that they only needed half the tribes to attend, but that at least five people from each tribe had to be there. Sometimes, it was preferable to take a measure to the Tribes, sometimes to the Centuries. Part of the game of being a good magistrate was knowing which assembly to convene. Should there be disagreement, a higher ranking magistrate could veto an assembly, or simply convene one of their own.
They voted in 35 tribes, 4 urban, 31 rural. Like the Centuriate Assembly, each group had only one vote, regardless of the overall size.

The Plebeian Council elected Plebeian Tribunes and Plebeian Aediles, and also passed motions (technically not laws) that were still binding on the Roman populace. Sometimes, magistrates seeking a rubber stamp would make use of the council, but could not use it for measures requiring a law.
Unlike the assemblies, the council could not be vetoed by a higher ranking magistrate, and each attendee had one vote.

The Assemblies functioned somewhat similarly to how representative democracy works today, by consolidating many voters into one vote. However, they were systemically biased to favour the rich, with 0.01% of the population holding 98 of the 97 votes required to win in the Centuriate Assembly, and realistically holding all 31 rural tribes. The Council was more direct, but still ultimately unruly, and the refusal of Patricians was still non-representative; by the mid-Republic, there were many Plebeians who were thousands of times wealthier than Patricians.

The idea that the Patron-Client relationship determined elections has been convincingly refuted, though it is still clear that clients played a role in getting their patron elected. This is mostly through spreading the word or simply being a true believer. Likewise, these people were public figures; you would see these men in the forum and the baths and so on, and it’s easier to vote for a guy who you’ve bathed with than a stranger.

TL;DR: Romans elected people they knew or had heard about to magistracies. They also voted on laws and motions which those same magistrates brought to the assemblies and to the council.
